Swan Hunter illustrates the distinction: it retains naval architecture and specialist engineering work but no longer has a shipyard.

evidence.note: The panel discusses successive RFA classes at Harland and Wolff and shared systems, with a qualified positive response.
The exchange distinguishes inactive yard facilities from Swan Hunter's surviving engineering business.

segments.summary: Successive auxiliary classes could preserve a yard's workload and share machinery, but integrating the programme would remain difficult.
segments.question: Could Harland and Wolff become the main RFA builder, moving between ship types while sharing systems?
segments.answerShort: There is potential for that approach, although integrating the orders and common systems would be difficult.

segments.title: Roman strength came from logistics and standardisation
segments.body: The Roman legions are presented as effective because logistics, standardized equipment, discipline, and engineering let them sustain repeated campaigns. Roman armies could still be beaten in Germany, the Sahara, the Carpathians, Persia, and Armenia. Rome's advantage was the ability to return with another well-equipped force and keep it in the field for months. That persistence depended on builders and engineers as much as battlefield skill. The empire could also abandon a frontier when the tax return no longer justified the cost.

evidence.note: A comparison with the Confederacy leads to the Roman army's advantages in logistics, standardisation, engineering, equipment, and repeated mobilisation.
The panel notes that many opponents defeated Roman armies, while Rome's persistence and willingness to abandon unprofitable frontiers shaped the larger outcome.

segments.summary: Roman armies were repeatedly defeated, but logistics, standardisation, engineering, and the ability to field another force made the system unusually persistent.

segments.title: Dry docks, cannibalization, and Royal Navy readiness
segments.body: Both additional mobile docks and the uncompleted Portsmouth carrier dock would be useful because working dock space is already delaying Type 45 maintenance and other ships' return to service. Parts were repeatedly removed from HMS Daring to ready another ship, resetting Daring's own schedule. Treasury-driven just-in-time logistics treats stored spares as wasted money, but specialized low-production naval components lack the robust supply chains that make the original industrial model work. Infrastructure and inventory policy therefore create a readiness problem that repair labor alone cannot solve.

evidence.note: The viewer asks whether a mobile or land-based dry dock would help most, and Dr. Clarke explains the current dock-space bottleneck.
The answer describes parts availability, dock access, and repeated cannibalization of HMS Daring.
The panel contrasts Treasury just-in-time policy with the selective stockpiling required for specialized naval components.

segments.summary: The choice between mobile and fixed dry docks opens into the infrastructure and spare-parts bottlenecks behind long Royal Navy maintenance periods.
segments.question: Would a mobile dry dock or another land-based dry dock help the Royal Navy more?
segments.answerShort: Both would help, but the deeper readiness problem combines scarce dock space with inadequate stocks of specialized spare parts.

segments.title: Impero loses parts and dock time before completion
segments.body: Impero lost components to keep her damaged sister ships in service. The example names a rudder transferred to Littorio and auxiliary machinery sent to Vittorio Veneto. Moving the unfinished battleship away from Genoa reduced exposure after war with France, but returning her later would have been dangerous. A long period without docking left the hull needing cleaning, while inadequate space at Trieste delayed fitting out. Cannibalisation, relocation and dock shortages combined to obstruct completion.

evidence.note: Parts transfers to Littorio and Vittorio Veneto.
Relocation, hull condition and docking or fitting-out problems.

segments.summary: Impero illustrates how cannibalisation and scarce docking space can leave an unfinished battleship progressively harder to complete.

segments.title: Why Admiral Hipper wins by default
segments.body: Admiral Hipper is selected largely because the alternatives are the Deutschland class and problematic light cruisers. The comparison gives roughly 14,000 tons standard displacement against a 10,000-ton restriction, then invokes the more capable Des Moines as a measure of what a large cruiser could offer. Political committees are blamed for accumulating features without integrating them efficiently. German high-pressure machinery is also described as individually temperamental: nominally identical turbines and boilers could require different operating knowledge and parts. That lack of interchangeability increased the fleet-support burden.

evidence.note: The viewer asks for the best Kriegsmarine cruiser, and the panel selects Admiral Hipper by default while calling it inefficient.
The answer compares Hipper's displacement with Allied possibilities and blames design by political committee.
Dr. Clarke explains the individually temperamental German turbines and boilers and their differing part requirements.

segments.summary: The Admiral Hipper class is judged Germany's best cruiser only within a weak field, with displacement and machinery used inefficiently.
segments.question: What was the best Kriegsmarine cruiser class?
segments.answerShort: Admiral Hipper, but mostly by default; it was large, inefficient, politically overcomplicated, and burdened by temperamental machinery.

segments.title: What turns a regional patrol ship into a global one
segments.body: An OPV becomes globally useful when it can self-deploy beyond its home region. Hull volume that appears inefficient beside a more heavily armed foreign counterpart may instead carry food, fuel, spare parts, workshops, and crew facilities. Weapon count alone cannot capture endurance and independence, which are operational capabilities in their own right.

evidence.note: The viewer asks when an OPV or corvette becomes globally rather than regionally useful, and Dr. Clarke answers in terms of self-deployment.
The answer identifies crew facilities, spares, food, weapons, and fuel as the volume needed for independent deployment.

segments.summary: Global reach depends less on a quoted range than on the stores, people, fuel, and repair capacity needed to deploy without local support.
segments.question: When does an OPV, corvette, or frigate gain global rather than merely regional reach?
segments.answerShort: When it can self-deploy and sustain itself with enough crew capacity, food, fuel, spares, and repair support for operations beyond local bases.

segments.title: The Type 45 cost of designing without power margin
segments.body: The Type 45 carried useful volume for stores and global deployment, but its original machinery fit left too little power margin. Hot-weather operations raised cooling demand while added systems consumed more electricity, exposing a weakness naval architects are said to have warned about. The proposed alternative was to modify ships five onward during construction, temporarily keep the first four in cooler European waters, and then upgrade them. A full twelve-ship programme could have incorporated those changes in later hulls. This is the construction and refit sequence proposed in the discussion, rather than the programme that occurred.

evidence.note: Dr. Clarke contrasts Type 45 endurance space with the decision to install only the minimum power capacity.
The answer explains that engineers warned about the lack of margin and that later hulls could still have been altered.
The panel outlines how a 12-ship program could have incorporated modifications before cancellation.

segments.summary: Type 45 power problems illustrate the long-term price of meeting a specification without reserve capacity for hot climates and added systems.

segments.title: Why USS Samuel B. Roberts was repaired after mine damage
segments.body: The panel answers that pride and political signaling kept the frigate from being scrapped after the 1988 mine strike. In peacetime, repairing a badly damaged warship demonstrates that an opponent has not removed it from the fleet, even when restoration is expensive and the hull may never be quite the same. USS Cole and Pearl Harbor destroyers reconstructed around surviving material show the same impulse to preserve a ship's identity.

evidence.note: The viewer asks what prevented Samuel B. Roberts from being scrapped after striking an Iranian mine in 1988.
The panel identifies pride and the political value of returning a damaged peacetime warship to service.
Dr. Clarke compares the decision with reconstructed Pearl Harbor destroyers whose identities were deliberately preserved.

segments.summary: The survival of USS Samuel B. Roberts after striking an Iranian mine is explained as a decision about national resolve as much as repair economics.
segments.question: What kept USS Samuel B. Roberts from being scrapped after it struck an Iranian mine in 1988?
segments.answerShort: National pride and political signaling favored repair: returning the ship to service demonstrated resilience even when rebuilding was costly.

segments.title: The Deutschland class beyond the pocket-battleship label
segments.body: The Deutschland class should not be read only through its famous pocket-battleship or commerce-raider image. The ships originated as replacements for pre-dreadnought coastal defence vessels intended for Baltic service. Added endurance allowed them to operate as long-range surface raiders, but that capability did not erase the design's underlying purpose. Their rapid withdrawal from ocean raiding early in World War II exposes the difference between an added capability and a role for which a ship is fundamentally optimized.

evidence.note: Dr. Clarke describes the Deutschland class as replacements for pre-dreadnought coastal defence ships with added oceanic range.
He notes that the surface-raider role was curtailed quickly at the beginning of World War II.

segments.summary: The Deutschland class began as a treaty-era replacement for coastal defence ships before its range enabled an ocean-raider role.
